catalog_quote: A third and most serious problem for the stress analysis suggested above is that the domain for penultimate vowel lengthening (or stress) in ciTonga is not the Prosodic Word. ... As the forms in (5) below indicate, the domain for PL in ciTonga seems to be the same as in neighbouring languages Chichewa and Tumbuka. Assuming that vowel lengthening is indeed a cue for stress, the domain of stress in ciTonga must be the Phonological Phrase. This is because lengthening usually shifts to the penultimate syllable of the rightmost Word in a Phonological Phrase. [sec.3.3.3, p.54] In phrase-final position, Prosodic Words which I suspect are phrase-heads have penultimate lengthening. In phrase-medial positions, we have Prosodic Words with no penultimate lengthening or any other cue for stress. [sec.6.3.5, p.195] One of them is that the domain for tone is the Prosodic Stem. On the other hand, the domain for Stress Accent is the Phonological Phrase. [Mkochi 2017, p.119] In fact, this is not a word-level stress, and it is not yet clear if ciTonga has word-/stem-level stress. This is because lengthening usually shifts to the penultimate syllable of the rightmost word/stem in a phonological phrase, as shown in (34) below.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: tong1321 (Malawian CiTonga) is not in the catalog. The single title-works with stress in the title, Mkochi & Bickmore 2021 JALL 42(2): 253-277 (doi:10.1515/jall-2021-2021), is a closed-access tone paper (floating H docking onto prosodic-stem edges); abstract read via Semantic Scholar/Crossref, no OA copy exists (OpenAlex/S2), no stress content in the abstract — low acquisition priority. The best first-hand stress statements come from material already held by the project: Mkochi 2014 NTNU dissertation p. 194 (and pp. 3, 6) — stress cued by penultimate lengthening falls on the phrase-penultimate syllable, domain = phonological phrase; Mkochi 2017 SPiL Plus p. 119 — 'not a word-level stress.. not yet clear if ciTonga has word-/stem-level stress'; Bickmore & Mkochi 2018 p. 3 and Mkochi, Rodriguez & Bickmore 2022 p. 155 — penultimate vowel of the last word in a phonological phrase lengthens. only direct download was available.

new_statements.rule_in_words: CiTonga is a tone language (H vs toneless roots, two surface tones, TBU = mora, length not contrastive). Prominence is cued by vowel lengthening of the penultimate syllable, but its domain is the phonological phrase: only the last word of a phrase (hence any word in isolation/citation form) gets a long, 'stressed' penult; phrase-medial words show no lengthening or other stress cue. The author explicitly leaves open whether any word-level stress exists.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; a stem-initial 'Accent Foot' is posited on segment-preservation and tone grounds but the author states it has no lengthening or other phonetic stress correlate (p.55).
new_statements.exceptions: Monomoraic/monosyllabic verb phrases (kol-a > koo 'catch', mel-a > mee) surface with a lengthened FINAL syllable even when prefixed (ndi-ngu-mu-kóo), i.e. phrase-final rather than penultimate lengthening, attributed to final-vowel deletion applying after penultimate lengthening (diss. pp.3-5; Mkochi 2017 p.120). A word-final H retracts to the second mora of the lengthened penult phrase-finally but stays final phrase-medially (Mtenje 1994 p.66-67).
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase-level: penultimate lengthening targets the penult of the phonological phrase (last word); citation forms are one-word phrases and so show penultimate length. Word-level stress explicitly undetermined per source. Variety described: Nkhata-Bay ciTonga, author a native speaker.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Malawian Tonga / CiTonga (chiTonga) of Nkhata Bay District, northern Malawi (Glottolog tong1321, ISO tog, Guthrie N.15); Mkochi 2014 specifies the Nkhata-Bay variety (author native speaker). Not to be confused with Zambian Tonga (tong1318, M.64; Goldsmith 1984 'Tone and accent in Tonga' is about the Zambian language) or Tonga of Mozambique (GiTonga, S.62).

new_statements.quote: Stress Accent in ciTonga belongs to the Phonological Phrase and it is assigned to the most salient position of the phrase, the phrase-penultimate syllable (somehow guided by the Universal Guidelines of EDGENESS and FINALITY). On the other hand, Strong Accent Feet belong exclusively to the Prosodic Stem. [...] The Stress Accent Bearing Unit is undisputably the syllable and it is cued by vowel lengthening.
new_statements.citation: Mkochi, Winfred. 2014. Strong Accent Constituents in CiTonga (Bantu): Universal Guidelines and Constraints. Doctoral thesis, NTNU Trondheim, 230 pp.
new_statements.locator: §6.3.4 'Stress Accent vs. Strong Accent', p. 194 (p. 214); supporting §1.1 pp. 3 and 6 (pp. 23, 26)
new_statements.reading: First-hand (native-speaker) statement: CiTonga stress falls on the penultimate syllable, realized as penultimate vowel lengthening, but its domain is the phonological phrase — lengthening shifts to the penult of the rightmost word in the phrase (le.lee.s-a 'look' / le.le.s-a vi-.βaa-.ntho 'look at bad people'), so it is phrasal rather than lexical word stress; Mkochi 2017 (p. 119) adds that it is 'not yet clear if ciTonga has word-/stem-level stress'. For a word-stress catalog: penultimate (phrase-level) prominence; word-level stress not established. The JALL 2021 title item is tone-only and adds nothing on stress.

tone_statements.quote: Malawian CiTonga preserves the Proto-Bantu two-way underlying tonal contrast. Like many Bantu languages, only high tones are active in the language because they can be the triggers or targets of tonological processes. I will assume, therefore, that the underlying distinction in the language is high tone (H) vs. toneless ([Ø], rather than H vs. L (low tone)). ... In (6a), where the root used is toneless, there is only one underling high tone, the melodic high tone, also known as grammatical tone, which is believed to be sponsored by the final vowel suffix (FV). ... It links with the stem-initial mora when it is the only tone in the verb stem, and then spreads once to the following mora.

sources.note: Ch.1.2 (pp.2-6), 2.5 (p.19), 3.3.3 (p.54): heavy (long) syllables occur in penultimate position and are the cue for stress; a syllabic-trochee word-stress analysis (stress on the penult) is presented and then rejected because the domain of penultimate lengthening/stress is the Phonological Phrase, not the Prosodic Word (lengthening shifts to the penult of the rightmost word in the phrase; phrase-medial words show no lengthening or any other stress cue). Language has two tones (H vs toneless/L), contrastive in rare cases; TBU = mora. Variety: Nkhata-Bay.

sources.quote: CiTonga has lost the Proto-Bantu vowel length contrast. We propose that all underlying vowels are short, and posit a regular process that lengthens the penultimate vowel of the last word in a phonological phrase.

sources.citation: Mkochi, Winfred. 2017. Resolving verbal reduplication paradoxes in Malawian Tonga. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 52: 101-126. doi:10.5842/52-0-726
sources.quote: p. 119: "In many Bantu languages, penultimate lengthening (PL) of the vowel is viewed as a cue for phrasal stress (also referred to as \"phonological phrasing\") (Downing 2004, 2006a; Kanerva 1990). In fact, this is not a word-level stress, and it is not yet clear if ciTonga has word-/stem-level stress. This is because lengthening usually shifts to the penultimate syllable of the rightmost word/stem in a phonological phrase"; p. 121: "confirming that phrasal stress is assigned to the rightmost word in a phrase."
sources.note: Sec.5 pp.119-121: penultimate lengthening in ciTonga is phrase-penultimate and cues phrasal stress assigned to the rightmost word of a phonological phrase; 'this is not a word-level stress, and it is not yet clear if ciTonga has word-/stem-level stress'; monosyllabic phrases (koo 'catch') get final lengthening.

sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.quote: In CiTonga, a Bantu language spoken in northern Malawi, multiple morphemes within the verbal complex sponsor High tone. Pre-stem High tones are underlyingly pre-linked, while those after the stem's beginning are underlyingly floating. These floating High tone autosegments dock exclusively onto initial and final tone-bearing units of the prosodic stem—a domain exceeding the morphological stem to include enclitics. Docking follows an edge-in process ... constituting a rare tonological motivation for the prosodic stem.
